newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA END-JULY DOMESTIC DEBT UP TO 3.9TRLN LEVS. [CORRECTED 16:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA END-JULY DOMESTIC DEBT UP TO 3.9TRLN LEVS. [CORRECTED 16:45 GMT]

text.p: Bulgaria's domestic debt rose to 3.978 trillion levs on July 31 from 3.789 trillion levs at end-June due to the lev's fall against the dollar, preliminary Finance Ministry figures showed.

"The rise amounted to some 188 billion levs. It was mainly due to the fall in the lev, which boosted the lev price of dollar-denominated domestic debt," a Finance ministry official, who declined to be named told Reuters.
The lev's decline against the dollar in July boosted the lev value of dollar-denominated government debt by 181.3 billion levs, figures showed.
The lev fell to 1,843.8 per dollar on July 31 from 1,718.6 on June 30 in the central bank daily fixing used in the calculations.
The government's direct borrowing from financial institutions stood at 1.2 trillion levs at end-July, up from 1.144 trillion levs a month earlier.

On June 30 the central bank wrote off the debt owed to it by the government, including principal and interest. On the same day a new debt to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) was issued, amounting to 482.2 million Special Drawing Rights to cover payments to the IMF.
The new debt is held by the central bank and is part of its Banking Department assets.

The restructuring was part of preparations to introduce on July 1 the IMF-prescribed currency board system, a form of fixed exchange rate mechanism aimed at stabilising the economy and boosting financial discipline.

The system requires levs in circulation, government and bank deposits and current accounts to be fully covered by central bank foreign exchange reserves and bans the central bank from lending to the government and commercial banks.
The lev was pegged at 1,000 per mark as an anchor currency under the currency board mechanism.

The dollar-denominated debt included $50 million of 18-month, floater coupon T-notes placed by the Finance Ministry with the country's state-owned Bulbank in April under a stabilisation plan for the ailing Biochimbank.
Dollar-denominated deposit guarantee bonds with a par value of $56.7 million were also in circulation at end-July, figures showed.

They were part of a total of $79.2 million worth of floater coupon T-bonds issued last year to guarantee foreign currency deposits of companies and individuals in five local banks against which the central bank has filed insolvency suits.
Another part of the debt was made up of bad debt bonds worth $892 million and 13.5 billion levs that were in circulation at end-July.
